content_html:
06.11.2026

As you may be aware, one of the limitations of musl-based distributions is that they will not function to their proper extent when used in computers with various NVIDIA graphics cards.

This is due to the proprietary nature of the driver, being built for glibc. I have been experimenting with trying to make this work, and this post is the summary of that effort.

Context

The NVIDIA graphics cards are tricky on Linux. While most other GPU vendors by default use free software graphics drivers (with kernel drivers in-tree in Linux, and userspace supplied by the Mesa project), NVIDIA in general does not, relying on an out of tree kernel driver and proprietary userland libraries that are supplied by the vendor.

A free software driver does exist, called Nouveau (kernel and OpenGL Mesa driver) and NVK (Vulkan driver). This allows the cards to work, but usually with significantly reduced performance, due to various reasons.

Currently the state depends significantly on what generation of NVIDIA card you have.

In short:

  • Anything older than Maxwell (GTX 700 series) is unsupported by the proprietary driver on modern systems, and supported to some extent by Nouveau, but may have issues due to poor maintenance nowadays; performance should be okay when it works.
  • Maxwell (GTX 700 and 900 series) and Pascal (GTX 1000 series) is supported fully by the legacy 580 branch of the proprietary driver, which also supports newer hardware. It works with Nouveau, but with very poor performance, as the cards can never reclock from their very low boot clocks (which would require firwmare that NVIDIA never released).
  • Turing (GTX 1600 series and RTX 2000 series) and anything newer is supported by the current main proprietary driver branch (at the time of writing, 620) as well as the legacy (580) branch, and by Nouveau, as these cards use the GSP firmware that is included in linux-firmware. However, using the FOSS driver means only getting 40-80% of the proprietary driver’s performance. Other than that, the experience is often okay, particularly with NVK.

In even shorter, if you have RTX 2000 and above you are mostly okay with FOSS but lose performance, if you have newer than GTX 600 but older than GTX 1600 you are screwed and need the proprietary driver, if your card is really old it may or may not work well and you may not be able to use it at all.

Proprietary drivers and musl

We now have a pull request open for both the 580 and 620 branch. It is not yet entirely ready but works, and is available for x86_64 and aarch64 architectures as NVIDIA supplies it.

To get there, there were multiple things to take care of. Particularly, using stock musl is out of the question and will likely never work. I will elaborate on each thing.

GLVND

The GLVND library was created by NVIDIA to allow for vendor-neutral OpenGL dispatch. It provides the libraries that applications link and exposes the OpenGL (and other) API. It then dispatches the calls to the implementations, which may be e.g. Mesa or the proprietary driver.

Most distributions nowadays use GLVND. Mesa comes with its own builtin dispatch code and does not necessarily require GLVND if you don’t build it with it. Musl distributions in general use this. Chimera at this point does not, and Void Linux on musl does not as it shares packaging with the glibc branch.

Chimera switched to GLVND on November 5 2026. Switching is rather straightforward and does not need much documentation. One just has to package GLVND, rebuild Mesa with it (to avoid using its builtin dispatch libraries) and take care of packages that have dependencies on mesa-devel.

GLVND is not only useful for NVIDIA drivers, but in general it is the primary thing users will find useful. There are also some vendor drivers on ARM and elsewhere but those are niche. The proprietary drivers mandate GLVND since many years back (this is also very useful on laptops with hybrid graphics, because then you may still want to keep Mesa for the iGPU).

Gcompat

The gcompat project provides a compatibility shim to allow for limited usage of programs linked with glibc.

It consists of two components:

  • the loader, which acts as the dynamic linker (ldso) for the programs. For example, on x86_64, glibc programs expect ld-linux-x86_64.so.2 as their dynamic linker. The loader does not do much, as it only sets up a library preload for the below, and execs into the real musl one.
  • the shim library, libgcompat.so.0, which implements various symbols that are in glibc and used by programs, but not in musl. It does not implement everything. It is what provides the bulk of the functionality, and is useed by the means of LD_PRELOAD, automatically by the loader.

Unfortunately for us, the latest tagged release of gcompat does not provide all the symbols the proprietary drivers require to resolve. Fortunately for us, the latest Git branch does. The development nowadays is very slow so we just bumped it up to the latest revision.

Patchelf and initial packaging

You can see how the packaging works in the pull request, and that part is rather unimportant for now, and does not require elaboration. It works in a similar way to other distros, downloading the .run archive from NVIDIA and installing everything to the correct places.

Of course, in our case, we cannot install it directly, because it depends on glibc and other stuff. We also can’t just pull in gcompat as is, because most of the driver is libraries that have no interpreter.

Let’s see what happens if we run ldd on libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07, which is the core OpenGL library.

There is a bunch of stuff here. So the libm.so.6, libc.so.6, libdl.so.2 etc resolve to ldd as they are reserved in the musl ldso:

static const char reserved[] = "c.pthread.rt.m.dl.util.xnet.";

The dynamic linker will ignore the suffixes.

For some reason, some of the libraries also have DT_NEEDED on ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 which is the glibc dynamic linker. There are also some relocation failures that we’ll get to later, for now we take out patchelf.

So, patchelf is a tool that lets you dynamically patch ELF files for things like library dependencies (DT_NEEDED), dynamic linker (DT_INTERP), RPATH, and even some funky dynamic symbol remapping.

We use this to sanitize every library and executable being installed. Let’s begin with something like the following:

$ patchelf --remove-needed ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 \
    --remove-needed libdl.so.2 --remove-needed libm.so.6 \
    --remove-needed libpthread.so.0 --remove-needed librt.so.1 \
    --replace-needed libc.so.6 libc.so \
    --add-needed libgcompat.so.0 libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07

What this does is drop all the dependencies we don’t need (this is optional as musl ignores them, but why not? And even on glibc since recent versions they are just compatibility symlinks that point to the libc itself) as well as add a new dependency on libgcompat.so.0 to supply the symbols.

This clears up the list a lot, and now only one error remains:

Error relocating libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07: unsupported relocation type 37

We will get to this below. You now have a rough idea about patchelf.

So, about that relocation 37

What is this? Let’s check elf.h.

$ grep R_X86_64 /usr/include/elf.h|grep 37
#define R_X86_64_IRELATIVE	37

Googling for this tells us that it’s a relocation type for GNU indirect function (ifunc). Ifunc is a mechanism for dispatching to different versions of a function based on a runtime condition. It is done by having a resolver function which does the decision logic, and returns the implementation, which is then called. A good writeup is here.

This is intentionally not implemented in musl. In glibc it is used to pick different implementations of functions like memcpy based on CPU microarchitecture levels for performance reasons. However, indirect functions are also a major attack vector, bypassing RELRO among other things, and in general there are other ways to do runtime dispatch anyway.

I remembered that there was a project called Alpaquita Linux which is basically Alpine with performance patches. It has the musl-perf package which provides a patched musl with string functions (and other things) from glibc and for this it also has patches for ifunc. We don’t need all of them, particularly the one for static linking is useless for us, so we take the one we need and its aarch64 counterpart for a good measure.

This just adds handling of the relocation. We then package the patched libc as musl-nvidia and poof, unsupported relocation is gone.

There are now no errors in ldd. That means we’re done, right? Nope :)

Thread-local storage

Oh boy.

So, about TLS. Normally, when you use OpenGL in an application, the implementation is dynamically loaded at runtime, not linked to the application. The OpenGL functions you use are then dynamically requested, usually through a portable wrapper (e.g. SDL_GL_GetProcAddress).

There are various TLS models. You can read up on them here. Look at the DT_FLAGS for the glcore and tls libraries. See the STATIC_TLS?

We have initial-exec, and our TLS needs to exist at a fixed offset from the thread pointer. This in general precludes dynamic allocation of the TLS memory. A quick test:

q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cat dynlib.c
#include <stdio.h>

__thread void *init_ptr __attribute__((tls_model("initial-exec")));

void upd(void) {
    init_ptr = (void *)0xDEADBEEF;
}
q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cc dynlib.c -o dynlib.so -shared -fPIC
q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cat test.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <dlfcn.h>

typedef void (*func_t)(void);

int main(void) {
    void *p = dlopen("/home/q66/dynlib.so", RTLD_LAZY);
    printf("SO %p %s\n", p, dlerror() ?: "");
    func_t upd = (func_t)dlsym(p, "upd");
    upd();
}
q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cc test.c -o test
q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ ./test
SO 0 Error relocating /home/q66/dynlib.so: init_ptr: initial-exec TLS resolves \
    to dynamic definition in /home/q66/dynlib.so
zsh: segmentation fault  ./test
q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ LD_PRELOAD=/home/q66/dynlib.so ./test
SO 0x700c30811080

When trying to use the driver, we would get the exact same error when trying to open the GL implementation. On glibc it works because it reserves some extra space in its static TLS at the beginning and gives them out for as long as there is space. It is limited, but enough for the driver.

The correct thing here would be to use TLSDESC (-mtls-dialect=gnu2) which is efficient enough and allows for dynamic TLS allocation, but NVIDIA apparently uses some rather old toolchains.

Since we don’t want to globally preload libnvidia-glcore into each process, I ended up patching the dynamic linker to handle this scenario with the same approach. I will not elaborate on the details of the patch as you can see it in the linked pull request and it is commented. It boils down to checking if the library has DF_STATIC_TLS in DT_FLAGS during dlopen and if so, checking if we have enough space for its whole TLS image in the spare memory, and if yes, avoiding allocating dynamic TLS for it.

That allows the above example to work without LD_PRELOAD.

(Another approach could be placing the TLS symbol definitions in something that is not runtime-loaded, e.g. placed into libGL or something else, and interposing the definitions; this could theoretically avoid patching the libc for this specific thing, but we have the ifunc thing too).

Procuring some hardware

I do not have any NVIDIA hardware. Before I could test, I would need to put a computer together.

Fortunately, my girlfriend still had her old computer’s GTX 980 Ti laying around. It is only supported by the legacy driver, but good enough for now. I then obtained some random old computer hardware (i3-7100, some RAM and a board, etc.)

It resulted in this monstrosity.

I could finally try if this thing works.

Initial testing and static mutex initializers

After this, the packaging was seemingly complete and I went to do some testing on the hardware above.

Well, it turns out trying to start anything graphical would just hang. I ran ls with libnvidia-glcore preloaded and saw:

Hm, pthread_mutex_timedlock in libnvidia-gpucomp?

Inspecting the assembly revealed that it’s re-entering a lock. That suggested that this mutex should be recursive, and for some reason it is not. Then a friend remembered that glibc has static initializers for these, particularly PTHREAD_RECURSIVE_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP, while musl does not support static initialization, only via pthread_mutex_init, for this case.

How to deal with this? On glibc, the mutex structure is publicly visible, and has roughly this layout:

struct mutex {
    int lock;
    unsigned count;
    int owner;
    unsigned nusers;
    int kind;
    ...
};

Then the initializer looks like this:

enum
{
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_TIMED_NP,
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE_NP,
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK_NP,
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP
}

# define __PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER(__kind) \
  0, 0, 0, 0, __kind, 0, 0, { 0, 0 }

# define PTHREAD_RECURSIVE_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP \
 { {  __PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER (PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE_NP) } }

That means it’s initializing the structure with the kind field.

Meanwhile, musl mutex type is opaque:

typedef struct {
    union {
        int __i[sizeof(long)==8?10:6];
        volatile int __vi[sizeof(long)==8?10:6];
        volatile void *volatile __p[sizeof(long)==8?5:6];
    } __u;
} pthread_mutex_t;

The mutex type is encoded in the first integer:

#define _m_type __u.__i[0]

In this layout, the kind would look like this, mirroring the glibc structure:

#define _m_kind __u.__i[4]

I found that musl does not use this in any way, however.

We can use this. The strategy I took was creating a new shim library containing the following:

int __nvcompat_mutex_lock(pthread_mutex_t *m) {
    patch_mutex_kind(m);
    return pthread_mutex_lock(m);
}

int __nvcompat_mutex_timedlock(
    pthread_mutex_t *restrict m,
    const struct timespec *restrict at
) {
    patch_mutex_kind(m);
    return pthread_mutex_timedlock(m, at);
}

int __nvcompat_mutex_trylock(pthread_mutex_t *m) {
    patch_mutex_kind(m);
    return pthread_mutex_trylock(m);
}

The patch_mutex_kind fetches the (on musl, unused) kind field and writes it into the type field`, atomically, if it’s unset. On statically initialized mutexes, it is always unset, as it’s only written once, and the static initializer for the default mutex just zeroes everything.

The actual encoding of the type is the same between both libcs (with the caveat that glibc also supports adaptive mutexes, which we map to regular ones), so there is not much remapping to be done. You can see the code in the pull request.

How do we use these symbols? Via patchelf again. It supports --rename-dynamic-symbols, which takes a mapping file where each line looks like oldsym newsym. We just provide ours like this:

pthread_mutex_lock __nvcompat_mutex_lock
pthread_mutex_timedlock __nvcompat_mutex_timedlock
pthread_mutex_trylock __nvcompat_mutex_trylock

Then we patch our libnvcompat into NEEDED of all the libraries.

And that’s mostly all.

Open-source components

There are various bits and pieces NVIDIA has released over time as actual FOSS code. This includes nvidia-xconfig, nvidia-settings, nvidia-modprobe, nvidia-persistenced, and the egl-gbm and egl-wayland external platform libraries.

These come bundled in the driver archive. Since they can be built from source, we package them separately, to minimize the amount of stuff that needs to be shimmed, and then depend on the from the driver package.

Testing for real

Yes, it works.

For the 620 driver, we also had to replace libstdc++.so.6 in a couple places, where it was being used for the new operator. This is provided in an way that is ABI-compatible by libc++abi.so.1 so we just replace it.

The packaging will need some more refinement, and more testing will be needed. It was reported to me that the 620 driver works with RTX 3070 Ti. It was also reported to me that it works at least partially on AArch64.

But anyway, that’s it for this writeup.

Error relocating /lib/libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07: mallinfo: symbol not found Error relocating /lib/libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07: __strftime_l: symbol not found Error relocating libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07: dladdr1: symbol not found Error relocating libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07: gnu_get_libc_version: symbol not found Error relocating libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07: dlvsym: symbol not found Error relocating libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07: backtrace: symbol not found Error relocating libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07: unsupported relocation type 37 There is a bunch of stuff here. So the libm.so.6, libc.so.6, libdl.so.2 etc resolve to ldd as they are reserved in the musl ldso: static const char reserved[] = "c.pthread.rt.m.dl.util.xnet."; The dynamic linker will ignore the suffixes. For some reason, some of the libraries also have DT_NEEDED on ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 which is the glibc dynamic linker. There are also some relocation failures that we’ll get to later, for now we take out patchelf. So, patchelf is a tool that lets you dynamically patch ELF files for things like library dependencies (DT_NEEDED), dynamic linker (DT_INTERP), RPATH, and even some funky dynamic symbol remapping. We use this to sanitize every library and executable being installed. Let’s begin with something like the following: $ patchelf --remove-needed ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 \ --remove-needed libdl.so.2 --remove-needed libm.so.6 \ --remove-needed libpthread.so.0 --remove-needed librt.so.1 \ --replace-needed libc.so.6 libc.so \ --add-needed libgcompat.so.0 libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07 What this does is drop all the dependencies we don’t need (this is optional as musl ignores them, but why not? And even on glibc since recent versions they are just compatibility symlinks that point to the libc itself) as well as add a new dependency on libgcompat.so.0 to supply the symbols. This clears up the list a lot, and now only one error remains: Error relocating libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07: unsupported relocation type 37 We will get to this below. You now have a rough idea about patchelf. So, about that relocation 37 What is this? Let’s check elf.h. $ grep R_X86_64 /usr/include/elf.h|grep 37 #define R_X86_64_IRELATIVE 37 Googling for this tells us that it’s a relocation type for GNU indirect function (ifunc). Ifunc is a mechanism for dispatching to different versions of a function based on a runtime condition. It is done by having a resolver function which does the decision logic, and returns the implementation, which is then called. A good writeup is here. This is intentionally not implemented in musl. In glibc it is used to pick different implementations of functions like memcpy based on CPU microarchitecture levels for performance reasons. However, indirect functions are also a major attack vector, bypassing RELRO among other things, and in general there are other ways to do runtime dispatch anyway. I remembered that there was a project called Alpaquita Linux which is basically Alpine with performance patches. It has the musl-perf package which provides a patched musl with string functions (and other things) from glibc and for this it also has patches for ifunc. We don’t need all of them, particularly the one for static linking is useless for us, so we take the one we need and its aarch64 counterpart for a good measure. This just adds handling of the relocation. We then package the patched libc as musl-nvidia and poof, unsupported relocation is gone. There are now no errors in ldd. That means we’re done, right? Nope :) Thread-local storage Oh boy. $ readelf -a libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07|grep TLS L (link order), O (extra OS processing required), G (group), T (TLS), 0x000000000000001e (FLAGS) SYMBOLIC STATIC_TLS 113: 0000000000000000 0 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT UND _nv005tls 123: 0000000000000000 0 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT UND _nv000tls 205: 0000000000000000 0 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT UND _nv002tls 224: 0000000000000000 0 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT UND _nv001tls $ readelf -a libnvidia-tls.so.580.196.07|grep TLS L (link order), O (extra OS processing required), G (group), T (TLS), TLS 0x003d40 0x0000000000004d40 0x0000000000004d40 0x000000 0x000038 R 0x8 0x000000000000001e (FLAGS) SYMBOLIC STATIC_TLS 9: 0000000000000010 8 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT 19 _nv008tls 11: 0000000000000008 8 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT 19 _nv007tls 14: 0000000000000000 8 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT 19 _nv006tls 17: 0000000000000020 8 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT 19 _nv005tls 25: 0000000000000018 8 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT 19 _nv002tls 28: 0000000000000030 8 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT 19 _nv001tls 31: 0000000000000028 8 TLS GLOBAL DEFAULT 19 _nv000tls $ readelf -a libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07|grep TPOFF 00000000022f5f98 0000007100000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000000 _nv005tls + 0 00000000022f5fa8 0000007b00000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000000 _nv000tls + 0 00000000022f5fd0 000000cd00000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000000 _nv002tls + 0 00000000022f5fe8 000000e000000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000000 _nv001tls + 0 $ readelf -a libnvidia-tls.so.580.196.07|grep TPOFF 0000000000004fc8 0000001100000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000020 _nv005tls + 0 0000000000004fd0 0000000900000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000010 _nv008tls + 0 0000000000004fd8 0000000b00000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000008 _nv007tls + 0 0000000000004fe0 0000000e00000012 R_X86_64_TPOFF64 0000000000000000 _nv006tls + 0 So, about TLS. Normally, when you use OpenGL in an application, the implementation is dynamically loaded at runtime, not linked to the application. The OpenGL functions you use are then dynamically requested, usually through a portable wrapper (e.g. SDL_GL_GetProcAddress). There are various TLS models. You can read up on them here. Look at the DT_FLAGS for the glcore and tls libraries. See the STATIC_TLS? We have initial-exec, and our TLS needs to exist at a fixed offset from the thread pointer. This in general precludes dynamic allocation of the TLS memory. A quick test: q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cat dynlib.c #include <stdio.h> __thread void *init_ptr __attribute__((tls_model("initial-exec"))); void upd(void) { init_ptr = (void *)0xDEADBEEF; } q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cc dynlib.c -o dynlib.so -shared -fPIC q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cat test.c #include <stdio.h> #include <dlfcn.h> typedef void (*func_t)(void); int main(void) { void *p = dlopen("/home/q66/dynlib.so", RTLD_LAZY); printf("SO %p %s\n", p, dlerror() ?: ""); func_t upd = (func_t)dlsym(p, "upd"); upd(); } q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ cc test.c -o test q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ ./test SO 0 Error relocating /home/q66/dynlib.so: init_ptr: initial-exec TLS resolves \ to dynamic definition in /home/q66/dynlib.so zsh: segmentation fault ./test q66@asusbook: /home/q66$ LD_PRELOAD=/home/q66/dynlib.so ./test SO 0x700c30811080 When trying to use the driver, we would get the exact same error when trying to open the GL implementation. On glibc it works because it reserves some extra space in its static TLS at the beginning and gives them out for as long as there is space. It is limited, but enough for the driver. The correct thing here would be to use TLSDESC (-mtls-dialect=gnu2) which is efficient enough and allows for dynamic TLS allocation, but NVIDIA apparently uses some rather old toolchains. Since we don’t want to globally preload libnvidia-glcore into each process, I ended up patching the dynamic linker to handle this scenario with the same approach. I will not elaborate on the details of the patch as you can see it in the linked pull request and it is commented. It boils down to checking if the library has DF_STATIC_TLS in DT_FLAGS during dlopen and if so, checking if we have enough space for its whole TLS image in the spare memory, and if yes, avoiding allocating dynamic TLS for it. That allows the above example to work without LD_PRELOAD. (Another approach could be placing the TLS symbol definitions in something that is not runtime-loaded, e.g. placed into libGL or something else, and interposing the definitions; this could theoretically avoid patching the libc for this specific thing, but we have the ifunc thing too). Procuring some hardware I do not have any NVIDIA hardware. Before I could test, I would need to put a computer together. Fortunately, my girlfriend still had her old computer’s GTX 980 Ti laying around. It is only supported by the legacy driver, but good enough for now. I then obtained some random old computer hardware (i3-7100, some RAM and a board, etc.) It resulted in this monstrosity. I could finally try if this thing works. Initial testing and static mutex initializers After this, the packaging was seemingly complete and I went to do some testing on the hardware above. Well, it turns out trying to start anything graphical would just hang. I ran ls with libnvidia-glcore preloaded and saw: (lldb) bt * thread #1, name = 'ls', stop reason = signal SIGSTOP frame #0: 0x00007b0f72259376 ld-musl-x86_64.so.1`__syscall_cp_c(...) at pthread_cancel.c:38:1 frame #1: 0x00007b0f7225843f ld-musl-x86_64.so.1`__futex4_cp(...) at __timedwait.c:24:6 [i nlined] frame #2: 0x00007b0f7225841b ld-musl-x86_64.so.1`__timedwait_cp(...) at __timedwait .c:52:7 frame #3: 0x00007b0f72258526 ld-musl-x86_64.so.1`__timedwait(...) at __timedwait.c:68:6 frame #4: 0x00007b0f7225b6d3 ld-musl-x86_64.so.1`__pthread_mutex_timedlock(...) at pthread_mutex_timedlock.c:85:7 * frame #5: 0x00007b0f67c033db libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_a033b0 + 43 frame #6: 0x00007b0f67bd8036 libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_9d8000 + 54 frame #7: 0x00007b0f67bd980d libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_9d9710 + 253 frame #8: 0x00007b0f67c0340a libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_a033b0 + 90 frame #9: 0x00007b0f67bd7fe2 libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_9d7f60 + 130 frame #10: 0x00007b0f67bdcd5e libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_9dcce0 + 126 frame #11: 0x00007b0f675df237 libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_3df160 + 215 frame #12: 0x00007b0f6a598132 libnvidia-gpucomp.so.580.196.07`___lldb_unnamed_symbol_3397eb0 + 642 Hm, pthread_mutex_timedlock in libnvidia-gpucomp? Inspecting the assembly revealed that it’s re-entering a lock. That suggested that this mutex should be recursive, and for some reason it is not. Then a friend remembered that glibc has static initializers for these, particularly PTHREAD_RECURSIVE_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP, while musl does not support static initialization, only via pthread_mutex_init, for this case. How to deal with this? On glibc, the mutex structure is publicly visible, and has roughly this layout: struct mutex { int lock; unsigned count; int owner; unsigned nusers; int kind; ... }; Then the initializer looks like this: enum { PTHREAD_MUTEX_TIMED_NP, PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE_NP, PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK_NP, PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP } # define __PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER(__kind) \ 0, 0, 0, 0, __kind, 0, 0, { 0, 0 } # define PTHREAD_RECURSIVE_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP \ { { __PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER (PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE_NP) } } That means it’s initializing the structure with the kind field. Meanwhile, musl mutex type is opaque: typedef struct { union { int __i[sizeof(long)==8?10:6]; volatile int __vi[sizeof(long)==8?10:6]; volatile void *volatile __p[sizeof(long)==8?5:6]; } __u; } pthread_mutex_t; The mutex type is encoded in the first integer: #define _m_type __u.__i[0] In this layout, the kind would look like this, mirroring the glibc structure: #define _m_kind __u.__i[4] I found that musl does not use this in any way, however. We can use this. The strategy I took was creating a new shim library containing the following: int __nvcompat_mutex_lock(pthread_mutex_t *m) { patch_mutex_kind(m); return pthread_mutex_lock(m); } int __nvcompat_mutex_timedlock( pthread_mutex_t *restrict m, const struct timespec *restrict at ) { patch_mutex_kind(m); return pthread_mutex_timedlock(m, at); } int __nvcompat_mutex_trylock(pthread_mutex_t *m) { patch_mutex_kind(m); return pthread_mutex_trylock(m); } The patch_mutex_kind fetches the (on musl, unused) kind field and writes it into the type field`, atomically, if it’s unset. On statically initialized mutexes, it is always unset, as it’s only written once, and the static initializer for the default mutex just zeroes everything. The actual encoding of the type is the same between both libcs (with the caveat that glibc also supports adaptive mutexes, which we map to regular ones), so there is not much remapping to be done. You can see the code in the pull request. How do we use these symbols? Via patchelf again. It supports --rename-dynamic-symbols, which takes a mapping file where each line looks like oldsym newsym. We just provide ours like this: pthread_mutex_lock __nvcompat_mutex_lock pthread_mutex_timedlock __nvcompat_mutex_timedlock pthread_mutex_trylock __nvcompat_mutex_trylock Then we patch our libnvcompat into NEEDED of all the libraries. And that’s mostly all. Open-source components There are various bits and pieces NVIDIA has released over time as actual FOSS code. This includes nvidia-xconfig, nvidia-settings, nvidia-modprobe, nvidia-persistenced, and the egl-gbm and egl-wayland external platform libraries. These come bundled in the driver archive. Since they can be built from source, we package them separately, to minimize the amount of stuff that needs to be shimmed, and then depend on the from the driver package. Testing for real Yes, it works. For the 620 driver, we also had to replace libstdc++.so.6 in a couple places, where it was being used for the new operator. This is provided in an way that is ABI-compatible by libc++abi.so.1 so we just replace it. The packaging will need some more refinement, and more testing will be needed. It was reported to me that the 620 driver works with RTX 3070 Ti. It was also reported to me that it works at least partially on AArch64. But anyway, that’s it for this writeup.

06.11.2026

As you may be aware, one of the limitations of musl-based distributions is that they will not function to their proper extent when used in computers with various NVIDIA graphics cards.

This is due to the proprietary nature of the driver, being built for glibc. I have been experimenting with trying to make this work, and this post is the summary of that effort.

语境

The NVIDIA graphics cards are tricky on Linux. While most other GPU vendors by default use free software graphics drivers (with kernel drivers in-tree in Linux, and userspace supplied by the Mesa project), NVIDIA in general does not, relying on an out of tree kernel driver and proprietary userland libraries that are supplied by the vendor.

A free software driver does exist, called Nouveau (kernel and OpenGL Mesa driver) and NVK (Vulkan driver). This allows the cards to work, but usually with significantly reduced performance, due to various reasons.

Currently the state depends significantly on what generation of NVIDIA card you have.

简而言之：

  • Anything older than Maxwell (GTX 700 series) is unsupported by the proprietary driver on modern systems, and supported to some extent by Nouveau, but may have issues due to poor maintenance nowadays; performance should be okay when it works.
  • Maxwell (GTX 700 and 900 series) and Pascal (GTX 1000 series) is supported fully by the legacy 580 branch of the proprietary driver, which also supports newer hardware. It works with Nouveau, but with very poor performance, as the cards can never reclock from their very low boot clocks (which would require firwmare that NVIDIA never released).
  • Turing (GTX 1600 series and RTX 2000 series) and anything newer is supported by the current main proprietary driver branch (at the time of writing, 620) as well as the legacy (580) branch, and by Nouveau, as these cards use the GSP firmware that is included in linux-firmware. However, using the FOSS driver means only getting 40-80% of the proprietary driver’s performance. Other than that, the experience is often okay, particularly with NVK.

In even shorter, if you have RTX 2000 and above you are mostly okay with FOSS but lose performance, if you have newer than GTX 600 but older than GTX 1600 you are screwed and need the proprietary driver, if your card is really old it may or may not work well and you may not be able to use it at all.

Proprietary drivers and musl

We now have a pull request open for both the 580 and 620 branch. It is not yet entirely ready but works, and is available for x86_64 and aarch64 architectures as NVIDIA supplies it.

To get there, there were multiple things to take care of. Particularly, using stock musl is out of the question and will likely never work. I will elaborate on each thing.

GLVND

The GLVND library was created by NVIDIA to allow for vendor-neutral OpenGL dispatch. It provides the libraries that applications link and exposes the OpenGL (and other) API. It then dispatches the calls to the implementations, which may be e.g. Mesa or the proprietary driver.

Most distributions nowadays use GLVND. Mesa comes with its own builtin dispatch code and does not necessarily require GLVND if you don’t build it with it. Musl distributions in general use this. Chimera at this point does not, and Void Linux on musl does not as it shares packaging with the glibc branch.

Chimera switched to GLVND on November 5 2026. Switching is rather straightforward and does not need much documentation. One just has to package GLVND, rebuild Mesa with it (to avoid using its builtin dispatch libraries) and take care of packages that have dependencies on mesa-devel.

GLVND is not only useful for NVIDIA drivers, but in general it is the primary thing users will find useful. There are also some vendor drivers on ARM and elsewhere but those are niche. The proprietary drivers mandate GLVND since many years back (this is also very useful on laptops with hybrid graphics, because then you may still want to keep Mesa for the iGPU).

Gcompat

The gcompat project provides a compatibility shim to allow for limited usage of programs linked with glibc.

It consists of two components:

  • the loader, which acts as the dynamic linker (ldso) for the programs. For example, on x86_64, glibc programs expect ld-linux-x86_64.so.2 as their dynamic linker. The loader does not do much, as it only sets up a library preload for the below, and execs into the real musl one.
  • the shim library, libgcompat.so.0, which implements various symbols that are in glibc and used by programs, but not in musl. It does not implement everything. It is what provides the bulk of the functionality, and is useed by the means of LD_PRELOAD, automatically by the loader.

Unfortunately for us, the latest tagged release of gcompat does not provide all the symbols the proprietary drivers require to resolve. Fortunately for us, the latest Git branch does. The development nowadays is very slow so we just bumped it up to the latest revision.

Patchelf and initial packaging

You can see how the packaging works in the pull request, and that part is rather unimportant for now, and does not require elaboration. It works in a similar way to other distros, downloading the .run archive from NVIDIA and installing everything to the correct places.

Of course, in our case, we cannot install it directly, because it depends on glibc and other stuff. We also can’t just pull in gcompat as is, because most of the driver is libraries that have no interpreter.

Let’s see what happens if we run ldd on libnvidia-glcore.so.580.196.07, which is the core OpenGL library.

When trying to use the driver, we would get the exact same error when trying to open the GL implementation. On glibc it works because it reserves some extra space in its static TLS at the beginning and gives them out for as long as there is space. It is limited, but enough for the driver.

The correct thing here would be to use TLSDESC (-mtls-dialect=gnu2) which is efficient enough and allows for dynamic TLS allocation, but NVIDIA apparently uses some rather old toolchains.

Since we don’t want to globally preload libnvidia-glcore into each process, I ended up patching the dynamic linker to handle this scenario with the same approach. I will not elaborate on the details of the patch as you can see it in the linked pull request and it is commented. It boils down to checking if the library has DF_STATIC_TLS in DT_FLAGS during dlopen and if so, checking if we have enough space for its whole TLS image in the spare memory, and if yes, avoiding allocating dynamic TLS for it.

That allows the above example to work without LD_PRELOAD.

(Another approach could be placing the TLS symbol definitions in something that is not runtime-loaded, e.g. placed into libGL or something else, and interposing the definitions; this could theoretically avoid patching the libc for this specific thing, but we have the ifunc thing too).

Hm, pthread_mutex_timedlock in libnvidia-gpucomp?

Inspecting the assembly revealed that it’s re-entering a lock. That suggested that this mutex should be recursive, and for some reason it is not. Then a friend remembered that glibc has static initializers for these, particularly PTHREAD_RECURSIVE_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP, while musl does not support static initialization, only via pthread_mutex_init, for this case.

How to deal with this? On glibc, the mutex structure is publicly visible, and has roughly this layout:

struct mutex {
    int lock;
    unsigned count;
    int owner;
    unsigned nusers;
    int kind;
    ...
};

Then the initializer looks like this:

enum
{
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_TIMED_NP,
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE_NP,
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK_NP,
  PTHREAD_MUTEX_ADAPTIVE_NP
}

# define __PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER(__kind) \
  0, 0, 0, 0, __kind, 0, 0, { 0, 0 }

# define PTHREAD_RECURSIVE_MUTEX_INITIALIZER_NP \
 { {  __PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER (PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE_NP) } }

That means it’s initializing the structure with the kind field.

Meanwhile, musl mutex type is opaque:

typedef struct {
    union {
        int __i[sizeof(long)==8?10:6];
        volatile int __vi[sizeof(long)==8?10:6];
        volatile void *volatile __p[sizeof(long)==8?5:6];
    } __u;
} pthread_mutex_t;

The mutex type is encoded in the first integer:

#define _m_type __u.__i[0]

In this layout, the kind would look like this, mirroring the glibc structure:

#define _m_kind __u.__i[4]

I found that musl does not use this in any way, however.

We can use this. The strategy I took was creating a new shim library containing the following:

int __nvcompat_mutex_lock(pthread_mutex_t *m) {
    patch_mutex_kind(m);
    return pthread_mutex_lock(m);
}

int __nvcompat_mutex_timedlock(
    pthread_mutex_t *restrict m,
    const struct timespec *restrict at
) {
    patch_mutex_kind(m);
    return pthread_mutex_timedlock(m, at);
}

int __nvcompat_mutex_trylock(pthread_mutex_t *m) {
    patch_mutex_kind(m);
    return pthread_mutex_trylock(m);
}

The patch_mutex_kind fetches the (on musl, unused) kind field and writes it into the type field`, atomically, if it’s unset. On statically initialized mutexes, it is always unset, as it’s only written once, and the static initializer for the default mutex just zeroes everything.

The actual encoding of the type is the same between both libcs (with the caveat that glibc also supports adaptive mutexes, which we map to regular ones), so there is not much remapping to be done. You can see the code in the pull request.

How do we use these symbols? Via patchelf again. It supports --rename-dynamic-symbols, which takes a mapping file where each line looks like oldsym newsym. We just provide ours like this:

pthread_mutex_lock __nvcompat_mutex_lock
pthread_mutex_timedlock __nvcompat_mutex_timedlock
pthread_mutex_trylock __nvcompat_mutex_trylock

Then we patch our libnvcompat into NEEDED of all the libraries.

And that’s mostly all.

Open-source components

There are various bits and pieces NVIDIA has released over time as actual FOSS code. This includes nvidia-xconfig, nvidia-settings, nvidia-modprobe, nvidia-persistenced, and the egl-gbm and egl-wayland external platform libraries.

These come bundled in the driver archive. Since they can be built from source, we package them separately, to minimize the amount of stuff that needs to be shimmed, and then depend on the from the driver package.
